title: Thermoelectric Effect — 20 MCQs
description: 20 MCQs covering Seebeck effect, thermocouple construction & working, Peltier effect and thermopile devices. Options are shuffled each load.

questions.q: Seebeck effect describes:
options: Generation of emf when two dissimilar metals have junctions at different temperatures
Heat flow when current passes through a junction
Emission of electrons from a hot surface
questions.explanation: Seebeck effect: a temperature difference between two junctions of dissimilar metals produces a thermoelectric emf.

questions.q: Seebeck coefficient has units of:
questions.explanation: Seebeck coefficient (thermopower) is emf per unit temperature difference, units volts per kelvin.

questions.q: A thermocouple is formed by:
options: Joining two different metals to form a pair of junctions
questions.explanation: Thermocouple: two different conductors joined at two junctions; temperature difference produces emf.

questions.q: In a thermocouple measurement the measured emf depends on:
options: Temperature difference between hot and reference (cold) junctions and materials' Seebeck coefficients
questions.explanation: Thermocouple emf is integral of difference of Seebeck coefficients over temperatures; depends on ΔT and material properties.

questions.q: To measure temperature using a thermocouple one typically needs a reference (cold) junction because:
options: Thermocouple measures temperature difference not absolute temperature
questions.explanation: Thermocouples produce emf proportional to temperature difference between measuring junction and reference junction; reference temperature must be known.

questions.q: Cold-junction (reference) compensation is required because:
options: Instrumentation must correct for non-zero temperature at reference junction to obtain actual hot junction temperature
questions.explanation: If reference is not at 0°C, compensation (electronic or using an ice bath) is needed to get correct absolute temperature reading.

questions.q: Which of the following metals/pairs is a common thermocouple type (e.g., type K)?
questions.explanation: Type K thermocouples use chromel (Ni–Cr) and alumel (Ni–Al) and are widely used for general-purpose measurements.

questions.q: Seebeck coefficient can be positive or negative depending on:
options: Which metal has higher thermopower — sign depends on materials
questions.explanation: If metal A has greater thermopower than B the measured emf sign depends on which is positive; coefficients can be positive or negative.

questions.q: Thermopile is:
options: An arrangement of several thermocouples connected in series to increase output emf
questions.explanation: Thermopile stacks thermocouples in series (often with alternate hot/cold junctions) to amplify voltage for sensing.

questions.q: Application of thermopile includes:
questions.explanation: Thermopiles detect radiant energy (IR) by absorbing radiation to heat junctions and produce measurable voltage.

questions.q: Peltier effect is:
options: Heating or cooling at a junction when current flows through two dissimilar conductors
Generation of emf from temperature difference
questions.explanation: Peltier effect: when current passes through junction of dissimilar conductors heat is absorbed or released at junction depending on current direction.

questions.q: Peltier coefficient has units of:
options: V (or J/C) — heat per unit charge
questions.explanation: Peltier coefficient Π has units of energy per charge (J/C) and is often expressed as volts.

questions.q: A Peltier cooler (thermoelectric cooler) works on which effect?
options: Peltier effect (current produces heating/cooling at junctions)
questions.explanation: Thermoelectric coolers use Peltier effect: DC current creates heat pumping from one side to the other producing a temperature difference.

questions.q: If two thermocouple materials have Seebeck coefficients S_A(T) and S_B(T), the thermocouple emf between temperatures T1 and T2 is:
questions.explanation: Thermocouple emf is integral of difference of Seebeck coefficients across temperature range; if coefficients are constant it reduces to (S_A − S_B)ΔT.

questions.q: If Seebeck coefficients are approximately constant over small ΔT, thermocouple emf E ≈
questions.explanation: For small temperature span with nearly constant coefficients, emf ≈ difference in coefficients times temperature difference.

questions.q: Advantage of thermocouple over resistance thermometer (RTD) is:
options: Wide temperature range and fast response
Higher accuracy at low temperatures only
questions.explanation: Thermocouples cover wide ranges, respond quickly and are rugged; RTDs can be more accurate in limited ranges.

questions.q: Limitation of thermocouple measurement includes:
options: Nonlinearity of emf vs temperature and need for reference junction compensation
questions.explanation: Thermocouple emf is not perfectly linear; tables or polynomial fits and reference compensation are required.

questions.q: Thermocouple polarity is determined by:
options: Conventional current direction and material Seebeck sign (which end is positive)
questions.explanation: Polarity indicates which junction is at higher potential dependent on Seebeck coefficients; instrumentation must respect polarity for correct sign.

questions.q: A thermopile used as a radiation detector typically connects thermocouples such that:
options: All hot junctions are placed on the absorber and cold junctions on a heat sink, producing series voltage proportional to incident power
Hot and cold junctions are mixed randomly
All junctions are kept at same temperature
Thermopile is used as a current source
questions.explanation: Thermopile arranges hot junctions at absorber (heated by radiation) and cold junctions at reference temperature to generate cumulative voltage.
